title: SRE Standards: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, and Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
body:
Overview

This document codifies Redwood Inference SRE standards for defining and operating SLOs and error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review criteria, operational tooling expectations, and canonical runbooks. The goal is to provide a single, actionable reference for service owners and on-call engineers to keep customer-facing inference services within agreed reliability economics and to accelerate consistent post-incident learning.

Scope
- Applies to: Redwood public API, model-serving frontends, traffic routers, dedicated inference lanes, and core control-plane services (auth, billing, metrics ingestion).
- Excluded: experimental research clusters and personal developer sandboxes (use project-level guidance).

1) SLOs and Error Budgets

SLO taxonomy and targets
- Availability SLO (customer-visible request success rate): 99.95% monthly for production endpoints (P0 tier), 99.9% for P1 tier.
- Latency SLOs (tail and median):
  - p95 request latency <= 120ms for small models (seq <= 128 tokens) on hosted API; p99 <= 300ms.
  - p95 request latency <= 400ms for large models (seq > 1024 tokens); p99 <= 850ms.
  - Streaming endpoints: time-to-first-byte (TTFB) p95 <= 80ms.
- Correctness/quality SLOs: model-output regressions are tracked via automated evals; regression SLO is zero major regressions per release window (see Quality Guardrails doc).

SLO definition guidance
- Always document: metric name (e.g., http_request_success_rate), measurement window (rolling 30d, monthly), numerator/denominator, excluded sources (internal healthcheck traffic), and alert thresholds.
- Prefer multi-dimensional SLOs where necessary (by model, by region, by customer tier).

Error budget policy and automated responses
- Error budget = 1 - SLO (e.g., 0.05% monthly for 99.95% availability).
- Burn rate monitoring: we use a two-window approach (6h and 7d) with the following actions:
  - Green: burn_rate <= 1 (no action).
  - Elevated: 1 < burn_rate <= 3 => SRE on-call notified; investigate potential mitigations (routing, canary rollback, throttling non-critical routes).
  - Critical: burn_rate > 3 => immediate mitigations and paged to SRE/Service owner; consider automated throttling, fallback model routing, and capacity expansion.
- Governance: if error budget is exhausted for a service for two consecutive windows, feature rollouts are frozen and post-incident review required within 72 hours.

2) Capacity planning and forecasting

Forecasting methodology
1. Input signals: real traffic (90d historical), business contract commitments (Dedicated tiers), marketing events, new feature release plan, and model size/latency profiles.
2. Baseline calculation: calculate 95th percentile QPS and token/sec forecast for target horizon (monthly).
3. Safety margin: add 30% baseline headroom for hosted API and 50% for Dedicated on initial provisioning; safety margin adjusted based on historical variance and upcoming events.
4. GPU capacity mapping: convert token/sec to GPU-hours using model-specific profiles in quantization-profiles and bench results (see benchmarking-and-perf-suite).

Capacity playbook (high level)
- Monthly capacity runbook: owners run forecast, validate committed capacity vs utilization, and produce a capacity report with recommended purchases or autoscale policy updates.
- Burst strategy: short 15-60 minute bursts permitted via burst pools; ensure burst pool usage capped per-customer and observable in dashboards.
- Pre-scaling for events: for planned releases/marketing events, pre-scale 24-48 hours prior depending on expected traffic ramp.

Metrics and thresholds for capacity alerts
- Cluster-level GPU utilization > 70% sustained for 30m => Capacity review.
- Node-level memory pressure > 85% => investigate model placement.
- Queue latency p95 > configured SLO > trigger scaling policy.

3) Reliability initiatives and roadmap

Current initiatives (owned by Reliability Program Team)
- Tail latency reduction project: adaptive batching and prioritized KV cache warming (owner: Luca Moretti, timeline: Q3 2026).
- Autoscaler improvements: reduce scale-up timeouts and smarter pod warmup (owner: Sana Patel, timeline: Q2-Q3 2026).
- Multi-tier routing fallback: automated downgrade from L0 (high perf) to L1 (cost-optimized) models under constrained capacity (owner: Priya Rao, timeline: Q4 2026).
- Observability modernization: centralize traces and token-level cost telemetry into single dashboard and expose SLO burn-rate panel for every service (owner: Ari Chen, timeline: Q2 2026).

Success measures
- Reduce p99 latency by at least 20% for top 10 routes.
- Reduce frequency of critical error budget burns by 50% year-over-year.

4) Incident review standards and postmortems

Severity classification
- Sev1: Customer-impacting outages with >5% of traffic failing or total regional outage; immediate page to SRE and Eng leaders.
- Sev2: Significant degradation impacting key customers or important SLOs but partial availability.
- Sev3: Minor degradation or isolated customer impact; not paged but tracked.

Post-incident template (required within 72h for Sev1/Sev2)
- Incident ID: Redwood-YYYYMMDD-###
- Summary: one-line impact statement.
- Timeline: chronological bullet list with timestamps in UTC.
- Detection: who/what detected the incident (alert, customer report, automated test).
- Root cause: concise cause statement.
- Contributing factors: list of systems/processes that made the impact worse.
- Mitigation and recovery steps: what was done to restore service and when.
- Action items: owners, due dates, and status.
- Learnings and follow-ups: documentation updates, automation, testing, runbook changes.

Post-incident process
1. Immediate triage and runbook execution (on-call).
2. Declare severity and engage stakeholders.
3. Triage notes collected in incident channel; preserve logs and traces.
4. Full postmortem created and shared with stakeholders within 72h for Sev1/2.
5. Action items tracked in Jira with SRE label and linked to postmortem.

5) Operational tooling and dashboards

Standard dashboards (Grafana)
- Service overview: success rate, latency p50/p95/p99, error budget burn-rate (panel for 6h/7d), token/sec. (dashboard id: grafana/SRV_OVR/001)
- Capacity cockpit: cluster GPU utilization, node memory pressure, active model instances, queue depth (grafana/CAP_CKT/002)
- Incident ops: real-time alert stream, paged incidents, on-call rotation status (grafana/INC_OPS/003)

Alert standardization
- Alerts must map to runbooks and include: symptom, suggested mitigation, runbook link, and paging policy.
- Alert severities and thresholds are stored in infra-standards; avoid noisy p95 alerts--prefer p99 or error-rate-based paging.

Tooling integrations
- PagerDuty for paging; escalation policy: primary on-call for 15 min, then secondary for 15 min, then Eng manager.
- Slack incident channel auto-created by PagerDuty with retained incident artifacts.
- Metrics pipeline: Prometheus -> Cortex -> Grafana; traces via Jaeger/Tempo.

6) Canonical SRE runbooks (examples)

Runbook: High request error rate (5xx)
- Symptoms: service error rate >= 0.5% and SLO risk, alert `svc-errors-high` triggered.
- Pager: page SRE on-call (PagerDuty).
- Immediate steps:
  1. Check recent deploys: `git log --since=2h --pretty=oneline` and deployment timeline in CI.
  2. Check service logs for 5xx stack traces: `kubectl logs -l app=service-name --since=15m`.
  3. Query metrics: `sum(rate(http_requests_total{code=~\"5..\",job=\"svc\"}[5m])) by (instance)` and compare to baseline.
  4. If a recent deploy is suspected: rollback via CI pipeline (link in runbook) or scale down new revision: `kubectl rollout undo deployment/service-name`.
  5. If downstream dependency failing: redirect traffic via routing console to fallback (runbook link) and notify dependency owner.
- Recovery validation: verify success rate >= SLO within 15 minutes and close the page once stable for 30m.

Runbook: Elevated latency (p99)
- Symptoms: p99 latency > SLO for 10 minutes.
- Steps:
  1. Identify affected routes/models in Grafana panel.
  2. Check queue/backlog: `kubectl top pod` and queue metrics.
  3. Enable routing fallback to lower-latency model variant for non-enterprise traffic (console action).
  4. Temporarily increase replica count or weight-based routing to spread load.
  5. If GPU contention suspected, move hot models to hot-pool nodes (see placement procedure).

Runbook: GPU OOM / Node memory pressure
- Symptoms: OOMKilled pods, node memory >85%.
- Steps:
  1. Identify pods: `kubectl get pods --field-selector=status.phase=Failed -o wide`.
  2. Inspect pod events and container OOM logs: `kubectl describe pod <pod>`.
  3. Evict or cordon node if multiple OOMs: `kubectl cordon <node>` and `kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data`.
  4. Rebalance heavy models: update placement labels and restart workloads on higher-memory nodes.

Runbook: Control-plane degradation (auth, billing, metrics ingestion)
- Symptoms: increased 5xx across many services, or alerts from control-plane dashboards.
- Steps:
  1. Check control-plane health dashboard and logs.
  2. If dependent service is down, enable cached responses and degrade non-critical features (billing metering delay).
  3. Pager senior on-call engineering and product support.

Runbook hygiene and ownership
- Every runbook must have an owner, last-tested date, and test checklist.
- Runbooks must be exercised quarterly via game-days. Update runbook within 7 days after a related incident.

7) Governance and SLAs with product/GTMs

- SLA vs SLO: SLAs are contractual and require remediation (credits) on breach; any service with SLA must have a higher SLO (e.g., 99.99%) and dedicated runbook for SLA breach process.
- Product teams must review SLO changes during quarterly roadmap planning with SRE.

Appendices

Appendix A: Ownership matrix (examples)
- Public API (edge): owner: Platform API Team (oncall: platform-api@redwood.com).
- Serving runtime: owner: Eng Serving Runtime (oncall: runtime-sre@redwood.com).
- Capacity and autoscaling: owner: Eng SRE Capacity (oncall: capacity-sre@redwood.com).

Appendix B: Example alerts and thresholds (table format described)
- `svc-errors-high` | symptom: 5xx >= 0.5% | severity: page | runbook: link
- `svc-latency-p99-breach` | symptom: p99 latency > SLO for 10m | severity: page | runbook: link
- `gpu-util-high` | symptom: cluster GPU util > 70% sustained 30m | severity: notify | runbook: capacity playbook

Appendix C: Postmortem checklist
- Confirm timeline and artifact links (logs, traces, runbook exec notes).
- Validate action items and assign JIRA tickets.
- Schedule 1:1 follow-ups for cross-team actions if needed.

How to use this doc
- Service owners: adopt SLOs in the service README and register SLOs in the SLO registry (see infra-standards).
- On-call engineers: follow runbooks and escalate per the paging policy.
- Managers: review SLO health during weekly reliability sync and include capacity forecasts in monthly leadership review.

Contact and feedback
- For questions or to propose changes, open a PR to this Confluence page or contact the Reliability Program Team (reliability@redwood.com).

This document will be reviewed quarterly and after any Sev1/2 incident to ensure runbooks and thresholds remain current.
